name: Unfollowing comparison accounts

card.summary: Curating a feed to remove accounts that trigger appearance comparison; experiments link idealised imagery to body dissatisfaction, but unfollowing itself is untested.
card.note: Related experimental research is about viewing idealised images, not unfollowing.

quick.overview:
This practice means unfollowing or muting accounts that prompt unfavourable appearance comparison. It is placed in the wiki as a lifestyle step.

Experiments summarised on Wikipedia link viewing idealised images to higher body dissatisfaction, but no study found tests unfollowing as an intervention.
quick.mechanism: The reasoning is that less exposure to idealised content reduces appearance comparison, which researchers identify as an important factor.[1]
quick.risks: No physical risks. Evidence on effects of curation is absent, and long-term effects of content exposure remain unclear.[1]

lead: Unfollowing comparison accounts is the practice of removing or muting social media accounts that provoke unfavourable comparison of one's appearance.

Wikipedia summarises a systematic review of 43 experimental studies linking viewing idealised images on social networking sites with higher body dissatisfaction in young adults, with appearance comparison identified as an important factor.[1] It also reports that findings on body-positive content are mixed and long-term effects unclear.[1]
No study found tests unfollowing itself.

paras: Researchers such as Ferguson are cited as arguing that peer effects matter more than media effects and that media effects are overemphasised.[1] Measurement varies, with more than 40 instruments in use.[1]
No studies found on unfollowing as an intervention. Related experiments on exposure to idealised images and body satisfaction are summarised on Wikipedia.[1]
